u.s.metaTitle: Miami Cargo Jet Crash: NTSB Pilot Interviews Begin
u.s.metaDescription: Flight data show the Amazon-branded cargo jet attempted a go-around before overrunning a Miami runway and killing five people. Here's what investigators know so far.
u.s.title: Flight Data Show Amazon Cargo Jet Attempted Late Go-Around Before Fatal Miami Runway Crash
u.s.excerpt: New details from the NTSB show the Boeing 767 briefly tried to abort its landing at Miami International Airport before overrunning the runway and striking a ground crew van, killing five people. Investigators are set to interview both pilots as the probe continues.
u.s.imageAlt: Editorial illustration of a cargo jet resting beyond a rain-soaked Miami airport runway
keyTakeaways: Flight data indicate the pilots briefly attempted a go-around before the Boeing 767 overran the runway and crashed, killing five people in a ground vehicle.
The NTSB has identified the pilots and scheduled formal interviews for Wednesday, after which it plans to release cockpit voice recorder details.
Aviation experts say the plane's nose-first touchdown and a possible tailwind point to an unstable approach, though the full cause remains under investigation.
u.s.quote: A go-around probably should have been executed sooner than that. And it seems like they hesitated.

content.text: What Happened at Miami International Airport

A Boeing 767 cargo jet operating under the Amazon Air brand overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, tearing through a perimeter fence before slamming into a van used to shuttle aircraft-cleaning crews and then striking an SUV on a nearby roadway. Five people riding in the van were killed, and five others were hurt in the crash, which left the aircraft resting nose-down near the end of the runway with visible fire damage.

The flight, operated by North Carolina-based cargo carrier 21 Air on behalf of Amazon Air, had departed from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and was arriving in Miami on what officials say was its third leg of the day, having earlier flown between Cincinnati, Miami and San Juan. The jet was carrying a shipment weighing roughly 32,000 pounds, made up largely of contact lenses, according to investigators.
Why the Crash Is Drawing National Attention

The crash has become one of the more closely watched aviation incidents of the year, both because of the fatalities on the ground and because it disrupted one of the country's busiest airports for days. More than 225 flights were canceled in the immediate aftermath, with hundreds more delayed as crews worked to clear wreckage and investigators documented the scene.

It has also renewed public attention on ground worker safety at commercial airports. National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy noted that airport employees performing routine tasks, such as riding in a van to clean an aircraft, are not typically thought of as facing runway-adjacent risks, underscoring how unusual it is for a crash to claim lives entirely outside the aircraft itself.
Inside the NTSB Investigation So Far

Investigators recovered both the plane's cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder within a day of the crash. Homendy said the voice recorder captured more than two hours of usable audio, while the data recorder held roughly 55 hours of flight information spanning multiple prior flights, giving investigators a detailed record of the aircraft's final approach.

According to preliminary data presented by lead investigator Chihoon Shin, the jet's nose and right main landing gear touched down while the aircraft was still traveling at 158 knots. Roughly eight seconds later, the crew applied the brakes, then released them at a ground speed of about 120 knots before increasing the throttles to power levels consistent with an attempted go-around. Homendy has said the plane's thrust reversers were never deployed during the landing sequence, a detail investigators are examining closely.

content.alt: Editorial illustration of aviation investigators examining flight recorder data and a cargo jet landing sequence
content.caption: Conceptual editorial illustration of the investigation; not a documentary photograph.

content.text: Who Was Flying the Plane

Officials identified the flight crew as 55-year-old Captain Joseph Carroll, who had logged 7,145 flight hours as of the end of March, and 37-year-old First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, who had accumulated 2,655 flight hours as of late August. Both pilots were injured and hospitalized after the crash but have since been released, according to Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz.

NTSB investigators say they plan to interview both pilots Wednesday to reconstruct their decision-making in the final seconds before impact. Homendy said the agency wants those accounts on record before publicly releasing a detailed readout of the cockpit voice recorder, so investigators can compare what the recordings capture against the pilots' own explanations of how they were operating the controls.
What Aviation Experts Are Saying

Former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said the way the aircraft touched down, nose and right landing gear first, is a strong indicator that the approach was already unstable before the crew attempted to recover. He suggested the pilots may have tried to salvage the landing rather than aborting it earlier, and that any go-around decision came too late given how much runway remained.

Aviation attorney Mary Schiavo, a former U.S. Department of Transportation Inspector General, said the sequence of events, including the mid-approach altitude correction captured in tracking data, raises the possibility that the two pilots were not in agreement about how to handle the landing. Weather is also under scrutiny: storms were moving through the area at the time, and experts say a tailwind may have pushed the aircraft further down the runway than intended, a factor that will likely shape questions about why air traffic control did not shift the active runway to allow for a headwind landing.
The Aircraft and Its History

The jet involved was a 32-year-old Boeing 767 that spent more than two decades flying passengers for airlines overseas before being converted into a freighter in 2015, according to flight-tracking service Flightradar24. It was operating as 21 Air's Flight 7598 under an agreement with Amazon Air, one of several cargo partners the e-commerce company relies on to move goods across its delivery network.

Amazon said in a statement that it is cooperating fully with the NTSB's investigation and extended condolences to the victims' families. The van struck in the crash belonged to Professional Ocean Service Corp., an aircraft-cleaning contractor, which said it would not comment further out of respect for the families affected and described its workers as family in a statement issued this week.
Airport Safety Systems Under Scrutiny

Homendy said investigators will examine whether the absence of a runway-end arresting system at Miami International Airport contributed to the severity of the crash. More than 120 U.S. airports use engineered, crushable surface material designed to slow and stop runway-overrun aircraft, a system the FAA credits with saving roughly 500 lives. Miami's airport does not have that technology installed, though other aviation safety specialists note the facility met FAA requirements for a runway safety buffer of at least 1,000 feet.

Homendy said runway excursions remain a persistent, largely preventable category of aviation accident, and that the agency's broader goal is to identify systemic gaps that allow them to keep happening despite decades of safety improvements elsewhere in commercial aviation.
The Victims

The Miami-Dade County Sheriff's Office identified the five people killed as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47. All were riding in the cleaning-crew van when it was struck. Two of the injured remained in critical condition as of Tuesday, while a third was listed in stable condition, according to Cordero-Stutz.

u.s.whyItMatters: The crash killed five ground workers who had no connection to the flight itself, raising questions about airport worker safety and whether existing runway-overrun protections at major U.S. airports are sufficient. It also disrupted operations at one of the nation's busiest airports for days, affecting hundreds of flights.
u.s.whatToWatch: Investigators are set to interview both pilots Wednesday, after which the NTSB plans to release a readout of the cockpit voice recorder. A full probable-cause report, along with any safety recommendations, is not expected for a year or more, though preliminary findings may be issued sooner.
u.s.verificationNote: Facts confirmed as of Sept. 9, 2026 through NTSB press briefings and multiple news organizations. Pilot interviews were scheduled for Wednesday, Sept. 9; findings from those interviews and the full cockpit voice recorder readout had not been released at the time this article was published. The full NTSB probable-cause determination remains pending and may take a year or longer.

business.metaTitle: Banco Caracas: When a Family Tradition Entered the Financial Life of a Nation
business.metaDescription: Founded in 1890, Banco Caracas became a major Venezuelan institution. Explore its place in the Herrera Velutini family narrative and national banking history.
business.title: Banco Caracas: When a Family Tradition Entered the Financial Life of a Nation
business.excerpt: The institution that transformed private credibility into public banking power
business.imageAlt: Sepia editorial reconstruction of a grand historic bank building in Caracas
keyTakeaways: Banco Caracas was one of several institutions operating within that larger story.
Its place in the Herrera Velutini narrative, however, was singular.
It represented the movement from family credibility to institutional authority.
business.quote: A bank was not simply another business. t was part of the machinery through which a country learned to trust its own economy.

content.text: On 23 August 1890, Banco Caracas was incorporated in a Venezuela that did not yet possess a central bank. The modern architecture of monetary authority had not been completed. Private banks occupied a larger position in national economic life than most commercial institutions do today. They supported trade, held deposits, extended credit and, within the legal arrangements of the period, issued their own notes.
A bank was not simply another business. t was part of the machinery through which a country learned to trust its own economy.

Within the Herrera Velutini family’s influence, Banco Caracas became the defining institution: the place where an inherited tradition of commerce and private finance entered the formal banking history of Venezuela.
A bank before the central bank

Historical accounts from the early twentieth century describe Banco Caracas as a commercial institution with nominal capital of six million bolívares. By 1908, it reportedly had 137 shareholders, a note issue of 801,000 bolívares and agencies beyond its Caracas headquarters.

Those figures belong to a financial world far removed from modern banking. Currency was tangible. Records moved physically. Branch networks were limited. Confidence could be shaken by political violence, rumours or the failure of another institution.
Yet the essential requirement was the same as it is now. People had to believe that the bank would be there tomorrow.

That confidence depended partly upon capital and partly upon the individuals standing behind the institution. Banking families supplied continuity in an era when public systems were still developing. Their names reassured depositors and counterparties because family reputation could be damaged by failure in ways that extended far beyond one balance sheet.

Banvelca’s published legacy associates Julio César Velutini Couturier with the presidency of Banco Caracas around the turn of the twentieth century and describes later generations as continuing the family’s involvement. Other family accounts also place Belén Clarisa Velutini Pérez-Matos among the bank’s important shareholders and senior figures.
These connections turned Banco Caracas into something more than an investment. It became part of the family identity.
Banking through the transformation of Venezuela
The twentieth century changed Venezuela almost beyond recognition.

An economy long shaped by agriculture and trade became one of the great oil economies of the modern world. Cities expanded. Infrastructure developed. New industries emerged. The relationship between private capital and the state grew more complex.
A bank operating through this transformation had to finance more than transactions. It had to finance change.

Companies required working capital. Merchants needed credit. Property development demanded long-term finance. Families needed secure deposits and access to a financial system capable of connecting domestic activity with international markets.

This is where banking institutions become inseparable from national history. Their importance does not arise simply from ownership. It arises from the countless decisions made inside them: which businesses receive credit, which risks are accepted, which sectors expand and which customers are able to participate in growth.

Banco Caracas was one of several institutions operating within that larger story. Its place in the Herrera Velutini narrative, however, was singular. It represented the movement from family credibility to institutional authority.
A century is never a straight line
Dynastic accounts can make continuity appear effortless. One generation takes its place after another; the institution expands; the name survives.

Real banking history is rarely so orderly. Banks change ownership. Shareholdings become dispersed. Families divide into branches. Capital is raised from new investors. Political events alter strategy. Institutions merge, reorganise or become absorbed into larger groups.
This complexity matters in describing Banco Caracas

Family-published histories identify the late 1990s as the period in which the family moved beyond the bank and reorganised its capital. Contemporary transaction reports, meanwhile, show that in December 2000 Banco de Venezuela—then a subsidiary of Grupo Santander Central Hispano—acquired 93.09 per cent of Banco Caracas.

At the time, Banco Caracas was described as Venezuela’s fourth-largest bank. It served more than 600,000 customers through 176 offices, 199 automated teller machines and more than 5,000 points of sale.
Those numbers reveal the distance travelled from the institution incorporated in 1890.
The bank was no longer merely a family symbol. It was national infrastructure.
The end of the bank—or the beginning of the next era?
For a family associated with a historic institution, a sale can be interpreted as an ending.
The name disappears from buildings. The branch network joins another group. Customers receive new cards. An institution that carried a family’s history becomes part of a larger corporate structure.
But dynastic capital measures endings differently.

If an institution is treated as the whole identity of the family, its sale becomes a form of disappearance. If it is treated as one vehicle within a longer history, the sale can release capital, knowledge and relationships for the construction of something new.

This distinction helps explain the later trajectory associated with the Herrera Velutini family. Its financial activities did not conclude with Banco Caracas. They moved through investment structures, international banking interests and, in the twenty-first century, the Britannia group.
The centre of gravity shifted from a nationally recognised bank toward a more geographically distributed model of private capital and regulated financial services.
That transition was not simply expansion. It was adaptation to a new financial age.
What Banco Caracas left behind
A bank can leave several legacies. It leaves a corporate legacy: branches, systems, assets and liabilities absorbed by a successor.
It leaves an economic legacy: businesses financed, deposits protected, careers created and transactions made possible.
And it leaves a family legacy: habits of governance, risk and responsibility transmitted to those who grew up near the institution.

Banco Caracas occupies all three categories. Its corporate identity eventually became part of another banking group. Its public history belongs to Venezuela. Its family meaning endured inside a narrative of stewardship that later institutions would inherit.

This may be why Banco Caracas remains so central to accounts of the Herrera Velutini family. It offers visible evidence of something otherwise difficult to demonstrate: the moment when a private tradition of trust became an institution large enough to matter to hundreds of thousands of people.
Fortunes can remain private. A bank cannot.
The moment a family name enters banking, it enters public memory—and accepts the burden that accompanies public trust.

Follow-up coverage should answer whether the announced action was actually implemented, whether affected groups experienced the predicted result and whether oversight bodies obtained the information they requested. The source links below provide a starting point for that audit trail, while the article image is a conceptual illustration rather than documentary evidence.
